data.title: D1 v1: client creation (server) — the POST /clients nobody owns

data.to:
Gap found while planning AS-42 (cto-owen, 2026-09-02) and independently confirmed by the orchestrator: repos.clients.create has ZERO non-test callers. Twenty call sites exist, all in test files. AS-39 built the repository; AS-43 and AS-42 both accept a clientId and neither creates one. Nothing in the shipped application can bring a client into existence.

WHY IT FELL THROUGH. The milestone plan cut the Clients screen (row C-16) precisely BECAUSE clients are created inline from the invoice and contract screens. That reasoning is sound for the UI, but it left the server half owned by nobody: AS-39 stopped at the repository, and the two consumers each assumed the other end existed. The boundary filter did its job on the screen and the split between server and UI tasks lost the endpoint.

WHY IT BLOCKS. AS-47's empty-client state is reached on the very first contract a freelancer creates — Flow 1 step 8 — and AS-46's invoice screen has the same inline-create affordance. Both UI tasks will arrive at a server that cannot answer them.

DECISION ALREADY RECORDED, to be confirmed in planning (AS-42 plan section 11): ONE shared POST /clients, built once, used by both screens. Never two endpoints, and never folded into POST /contracts or POST /invoices as a nested create — a nested create makes client creation a side effect of a different resource and makes partial failure ambiguous. The default is that whichever of AS-46 or AS-47 lands first builds it; filing it separately here instead means neither UI task carries a hidden server dependency and the endpoint gets its own review.

SHAPE, for the planner rather than binding: the route sits below the auth boundary and takes its freelancer from the session, exactly as AS-42 and AS-43 do; ownership is enforced by the composite FK rather than re-checked in application code; the repository already enforces name and email validation and is already tested (AS-39 cases cover create, uniqueness semantics, and the FK). The plan should say what happens on a duplicate — AS-39 deliberately did NOT make client email unique per freelancer (see the states ledger), so duplicates are legal and the answer is probably to return the new row rather than to converge on an existing one, but that is a decision to take and record, not to assume.

ACCEPTANCE: the description's shape holds; ownership is engine-enforced and a cross-tenant attempt returns the same answer as a nonexistent parent; at least one falsification recipe breaks a guard this task introduces, shown red once per the house technique (assert the mutation applied on disk and in the built image, predict executable case names that exist, restore, prove restoration by content hash plus git status --porcelain, rebuild before re-running); the test service stays network_mode: none; no new dependencies; no migration (the table exists); no protected top-level file edited; no running container touched. Complexity low.

data.body:
Pulled as the top D1 pull: it is the only remaining high, its dependency (AS-40) is done, and it directly blocks AS-46 and AS-47 — the two UI screens that both create clients inline. Every other remaining D1 task is a UI task or the acceptance run.

Lena implements. Marcus wrote AS-42 and AS-43, the two consumers that take a clientId and assume this endpoint exists, so a fresh reader is more likely to notice if the endpoint's shape quietly diverges from what they assumed. She also built the auth boundary this route sits below.

Note for the planner, and it is the whole reason this task exists as a separate one: AS-39 built the clients repository and nothing ever called it. The endpoint fell between the repository task and the two UI tasks and was owned by neither. So the plan should state, explicitly, which task owns each half of a resource whose creation surface is split across a screen and a server — that boundary is what failed here, and AS-46/AS-47 will hit the same seam for anything else they create inline.

Plan written. Duplicate ruling: POST /clients unconditionally inserts and never converges — the schema declines the unique index on purpose (0001-initial.js: 'NOT unique: duplicate is a non-blocking warning') and the ledger requires 'create a new client anyway' to be an expressible outcome, which an upsert cannot express; a double submit therefore creates two rows, accepted, with no money and no external call behind it. Response is 303 to a REQUIRED, safeNext-validated return path carrying clientId=<new id> — required rather than defaulted because there is no Clients screen to default to and a default would silently discard the form the freelancer was filling. The route adds nothing the repository already does: no field allowlist (assertKnownKeys is the one that cannot be bypassed), no name/email check, no length ceiling. Ownership is actingFreelancerId as the first positional argument and the composite FK; there is no cross-tenant path INTO this route, which is stated and proven rather than papered over with an unreachable 404 mapping. Five falsification recipes, F1 falsifies the ownership scoping and F5 gives the composite FK the recipe it has been missing since AS-42. Also filed AS-67: client email format validation is missing one layer down and belongs in the repository, not smuggled into this route — which is the same seam rule this task exists to write.

Recording the §3.7 rule as a standing convention proposal rather than leaving it inside one task's plan, because it is the only artifact from this task that outlives it.

The rule: a resource whose creation surface is split between a screen and a server has three obligations with three owners — the row (the repository task), the ENDPOINT (a task of its own, filed when the repository task lands), and the states (the screen task). The endpoint is never inherited by "whichever screen gets there first". That default is exactly what produced this gap: two screens each assumed the other carried it, and the endpoint was owned by neither for four tasks.

The mechanical test is the part worth keeping, because it is checkable rather than exhortative: a repository write method with zero non-test callers at the end of its own task is an unowned endpoint, not a finished repository. Grep before done; every zero-caller method either names a filed consumer task or gets one filed.

Applying the test right now, to this codebase, finds a second instance: repos.clients.update still has zero non-test callers after AS-65 lands, and no consumer task exists anywhere in the screen budget. Owen raised it and deliberately did not action it — that is a CTO call he would rather make with AS-46 and AS-47 planned, which is the right sequencing. Recorded here so it is not lost between plans.

The wording is in the plan's §10 for the metawork layer to apply to CLAUDE.md. I am not applying it this tick: it is a convention change, not a task artifact, and the board should see it before it binds future tasks.

Starting implementation in .worktrees/AS-65 on feat/AS-65-clients, per the plan: unconditional insert with no convergence, a required and pre-validated next field composing the 303, the rest-spread that re-parents the null-prototype body before the repository's plain-object check, three-case taxonomy only, and the two ownership falsifiers the plan adds.

IMPLEMENTATION COMPLETE — commit 4762eb2 on feat/AS-65-clients (worktree .worktrees/AS-65, clean; nothing pushed, nothing merged).

FILES TOUCHED — 6, exactly §2's list, measured `git diff --stat master...feat/AS-65-clients`: 607 insertions, 10 deletions.
  routes/clients.js            +135 (new)
  test/clients.test.js         +444 (new, L1-L11)
  app.js                       +11  (one import at line 33, one mount + banner as item 13)
  test/auth.test.js            14 changed (8 literal edits)
  test/dependency-policy.test.js 8 changed (3 edits)
  test/harness.test.js         5 changed (3 edits)
Verified UNTOUCHED, one by one, the whole of §5.2 plus §4's none-claims: lib/db/repositories/clients.js, both migrations, lib/config.js, lib/db/errors.js, lib/auth/guard.js, routes/contracts.js, routes/invoices.js, test/{config,db,repositories,deploy-shape,contracts,invoices}.test.js, package.json, package-lock.json, Dockerfile, compose.yaml, CLAUDE.md, README.md, PHILOSOPHY.md, agents.md. No .lattice path in the branch diff (0). SCHEMA_VERSION is still derived from MIGRATIONS.at(-1) and the migration set is untouched.

THE PARSED BODY'S PROTOTYPE — THE PLAN'S §3.4 LOAD-BEARING NOTE IS WRONG, AND THE DESIGN IS UNCHANGED ANYWAY.
Probed inside the real image (express 5.2.1, body-parser 2.3.0, node 24.20.0) rather than taken on trust, POSTing a real urlencoded form through `express.urlencoded({ extended: false, limit: '32kb', parameterLimit: 20 })`:
  Object.getPrototypeOf(req.body) === Object.prototype  ->  TRUE
  Object.getPrototypeOf(req.body) === null              ->  FALSE
  assertPlainObject(req.body, 'raw')                    ->  ACCEPTED
So the body is NOT null-prototype and passing it straight to the repository would NOT 400 for that reason. Mechanism, read off the shipped source: body-parser 2.3.0's createQueryParser routes BOTH extended and non-extended through `qs.parse` (lib/types/urlencoded.js:99) — `extended: false` only sets `depth: 0`; it no longer uses node:querystring at all, and qs with `plainObjects` unset builds with `{}`. The plan's inference was correct for the older body-parser that did use querystring.parse.
The rest-spread stays, for the reason the plan gives independently: `next` is the router's field and must be split out or the repository's assertKnownKeys rejects it. That is what L1 actually catches — it 400s on `client.next`, not on the prototype. Second probe, worth knowing: with NO content-type the parser does not run and `req.body` is `undefined`, which is why the handler reads `req.body ?? {}`.

SUITE RESULTS — both services, from .worktrees/AS-65/apps/invoicing, isolated compose project `asc-inv-as65`.
  A) `docker compose run --rm test` (network_mode: none, unchanged): tests 380, pass 362, fail 0, skipped 18, ~5.8s.
     Baseline on the same tree before the change: tests 369, pass 351, fail 0, skipped 18. Delta +11 = the eleven L cases, each confirmed to have RUN by name in the output.
     SKIP SET, enumerated — all 18 carry the same reason, "ASC_STRIPE_MOCK_URL not set — run the contract service", and all 18 are pre-existing:
       connect.test.js  M1 start / M2 return / M3 refresh against stripe-mock (3)
       invoices.test.js M1 finalize / M2 send / M3 reconciliation guard against stripe-mock (3)
       stripe-mock.test.js: the mock is reachable and is not Stripe; strict version check is on; connected POST /v1/customers; POST /v1/invoiceitems; POST /v1/invoices; POST /v1/invoices/{id}/finalize; POST /v1/invoices/{id}/send; GET /v1/invoices/{id}; platform POST /v1/accounts, POST /v1/account_links, GET /v1/accounts/{id}; unknown parameters are rejected by the mock; Idempotency-Key is echoed and Request-Id surfaces as requestId; the mock ACCEPTS the forbidden shape raw (12)
  B) `docker compose run --rm contract` (the internal, egress-less stripe-mock network; image already local, no signup, no spend): tests 380, pass 380, fail 0, skipped 0. So the 18 are skips of configuration, not of capability, and nothing this task added depends on them.

FALSIFICATION — five recipes, each ONE INDIVISIBLE STEP against a `git archive HEAD` extract OUTSIDE the worktree (481 files), harness aborting on any failed assertion. Per recipe: content-hash manifest of the whole extract before mutation -> backup OUTSIDE the extract -> trap restore on EXIT -> mutate -> assert applied ON DISK (occurrence-accurate `str.count`, never `grep -c`) -> `compose build test` -> assert applied IN THE BUILT IMAGE by reading the file out of /app -> run -> record the exact failing set -> restore -> re-hash and diff the manifest (byte-identical) -> `git status --porcelain` on the task worktree empty -> REBUILD -> assert the mutant is GONE from the rebuilt image -> re-run green (380/362/0/18 every time).

  F1 ownership falsifier (identity source). `const freelancerId = req.body?.freelancerId ?? actingFreelancerId(req)` + `freelancerId` destructured out of fields.
     assert-applied: disk `body?.freelancerId` 0 -> 1, `freelancerId: _named` 0 -> 1; IMAGE both 1. Rebuilt image: 0.
     PREDICTED exactly one: L8. OBSERVED exactly one: L8 ("identity is the session's, and the minted id is inert for every other freelancer"). MATCH.
     Predicted-green spot-checked and green: L1-L7, L9, L10, L11, G1, G2, G3, all of harness.test.js, all of dependency-policy.test.js.
  F2 duplicate ruling. Converge on a findByEmail hit instead of inserting.
     assert-applied: disk `findByEmail` 0 -> 1, `existing.length > 0` 0 -> 1; IMAGE both 1. Rebuilt image: 0.
     PREDICTED exactly one: L3. OBSERVED exactly one: L3. MATCH.
  F3 return-path validation (open redirect). `const returnPath = safeNext(next)` -> `const returnPath = next`, import kept.
     assert-applied: disk `safeNext` 2 -> 1, `const returnPath = next;` 0 -> 1; IMAGE 1 and 1. Rebuilt image: 2.
     PREDICTED red: L6 AND L7. OBSERVED red: L6 ONLY (one case). NARROWER THAN PREDICTED — recorded as a finding per §7, see deviation 2.
  F4 route partition literals. `app.use(clientRoutes(config, { repos }));` DELETED from app.js (deleted, never commented out).
     assert-applied: disk `clientRoutes` 2 -> 1, `app.use(clientRoutes` 1 -> 0; IMAGE 1 and 0. Rebuilt image: 2.
     PREDICTED exactly fifteen. OBSERVED exactly fifteen: G1, G1b, G2, G3, G15, L1, L2, L3, L4, L5, L6, L7, L8, L9, L11. MATCH — and the fifteenth is G15, which the plan's §5.1 literal table omitted (deviation 1).
     Predicted-green and green: L10, V1, V2 (both), V4, and both dependency-policy inventory/concept cases.
  F5 composite FK. The `FOREIGN KEY (freelancer_id, client_id) REFERENCES clients (freelancer_id, id)` clause deleted from the contracts table ONLY.
     assert-applied: disk `REFERENCES clients (freelancer_id, id)` 2 -> 1 and `UNIQUE (freelancer_id, id)` 1 -> 1 (asserted UNCHANGED, so the mutation is the one intended); IMAGE 1 and 1. Rebuilt image: 2.
     PREDICTED exactly one: X5. OBSERVED exactly one: X5. MATCH. Predicted-green and green: X4, D2, D3, and L8 — so §3.5's design note stands: L8's cross-tenant half is refused earlier, by AS-42's owner check, not by this FK.

LITERALS THAT MOVED — every one in §5.1, plus one the plan missed.
  dependency-policy.test.js: source.length 48 -> 49 (and its message); 'routes/clients.js' inserted between 'routes/auth.js' and 'routes/connect.js'; `body parser` row widened to 5 entries with 'routes/clients.js' in sort position, and a three-line comment added saying AS-65 did so and why, matching AS-42's.
  harness.test.js: found.length 15 -> 16; "expected exactly 15 test files" -> 16; 'clients.test.js' inserted between 'auth.test.js' and 'config.test.js'; prose "these fifteen files ran" -> "sixteen".
  auth.test.js: ALL_ROUTES gains 'POST /clients' between 'GET /tokens.css' and 'POST /connect-stripe/start'; G1 found.length 15 -> 16 and its message; G1b found.length 14 -> 15; G2's inline protectedRoutes gains 'POST /clients' between 'GET /connect-stripe/return' and 'POST /connect-stripe/start'; G3 protectedRoutes.length 10 -> 11; G3 prose "nine" -> "eleven" at both occurrences (the AS-42 residual §11 item 1 names); AND G15 discoverRoutes(app).length 15 -> 16.
  NOT-MOVING SET CONFIRMED: every file in §5.2 is byte-identical to master (list above). routes/clients.js was measured against every concept row that could claim it: money words (amount|currency|money, RAW) 0, "stripe" (any case) 0, req.currentUser 0, console.* 0, and it names no createHash/randomBytes/timingSafeEqual/createHmac/STATUS_RANK/'platform: true'/node:sqlite/'/webhook'/STRIPE_.

DEVIATIONS (numbered, each the smallest thing that satisfies the intent)
  1. G15's `assert.equal(discoverRoutes(app).length, 15)` in auth.test.js is a moving literal the plan's §5.1 table does not list. Moved to 16 in the same commit. Not optional — without it the suite is red — and it is what makes F4's predicted count of fifteen come out exactly. The §5.1 table is incomplete by one row, not wrong.
  2. F3 reddened L6 alone; L7 stayed GREEN. §7 says to record this either way, and calls the green a finding. The mechanism is narrower than §7's worry: L7's inputs are by construction all values safeNext ACCEPTS, and safeNext returns accepted values unchanged, so removing the call cannot move L7 — it is a scoping property of L7, not the composition absorbing anything. The substantive half of §7's worry is nevertheless TRUE and worth writing down: under F3 a refused `//evil.test/steal` composes to `/steal?clientId=...` — app-relative, no host leak — because `new URL(next, base)` then taking pathname+search+hash discards the authority. So the composition IS a second, silent layer against an open redirect, and L6 (which asserts 400, not "no host in the Location") is the only case that notices the validator is gone. Left as designed; L6 carries it.
  3. FIRST F1 RUN PRODUCED A WIDER SET THAN PREDICTED (L8 plus dependency-policy's source-inventory case) AND THE HARNESS WAS THE CAUSE, not the guard: the backup copy was written as routes/clients.js.orig INSIDE the extract, the Dockerfile's `COPY apps/invoicing/routes ./routes` carried it into the image, and the scan correctly refused to classify it. Backup moved outside the extract; F1 re-run from a fresh extract gave exactly one. Recording it because "a wider failing set than predicted is itself a finding" and the finding here was mine.
  4. L10 deliberately does NOT assert app.js's mount line, where contracts.test.js's Y2 does assert its own. F4's predicted-green for L10 requires it: an assertion that the mount EXISTS would make L10 red under a recipe that deletes the mount, for a reason L10 is not about. L10 asserts the ABSENCE instead (`/clientRoutes\([^)]*stripe/` is false in app.js), which survives the deletion. The mount's existence and position are auth.test.js's G1/G2/G3/G15 to guard, and F4 shows all four do.
  5. L1 asserts the 303 carries no JSON body rather than an EMPTY body. Measured: express 5's res.redirect answers a `Accept: */*` request with an HTML "See Other. Redirecting to ..." body. "No body" in §3.3 means "no representation of the created object"; the non-JSON assertion is the honest form of it.
  6. Docker teardown left ~13 dangling intermediate images from my builds. Both tagged images I created (asc-inv-as65-test, asc-inv-as65-contract, plus the recipe project's asc-inv-as65-fx-test) are removed, no global prune was run, stripe/stripe-mock:v0.203.0 is left pulled, and asc-invoicing-web-1 (8348) and asc-chat-server-1 (8347) were never touched. The daemon already held 400+ dangling images before this task started and they are not attributable, so removing untagged layers by age would be exactly the "clean up unfamiliar state" instinct the shared-worktree rule forbids. Flagging rather than acting.

LEFT UNDONE, ON PURPOSE
  - §10's proposed CLAUDE.md wording (the split-resource rule) is metawork; employees do not edit that file. It is in the plan verbatim for the metawork layer.
  - §11 item 3: repos.clients.update still has zero non-test callers after this task. Raised for the CTO by the plan; not actioned here.
  - §9 Q4 (email format validation, belongs in the repository) is filed separately and is non-blocking for AS-46/AS-47, per the plan.
  - Q1/Q2 defaults are in force as written: `next` required, parameter named clientId. Either is a one-constant change if AS-46 or AS-47 needs otherwise.

FOR THE REVIEWER, FIRST: the parsed-body finding above (the plan's §3.4 rationale is stale for body-parser 2.3.0 — the code is unaffected, the note is not), then deviation 1 (the G15 literal the plan's table omits, and why F4's count of fifteen is the evidence it belongs), then deviation 2 (F3's narrower-than-predicted set, and what actually guards the open redirect).

Orchestrator verification and review assignment.

VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY: 6 files, +607/-10, exactly the declared scope, nothing outside apps/invoicing/, zero files under lib/db/ (so no migration and SCHEMA_VERSION does not move), and the money-word trap is clean — no banned token appears in routes/clients.js, comments included.

THE PROTOTYPE FINDING IS THE VALUABLE ONE, and it goes the opposite way from the plan. The plan warned that the parsed body has a null prototype and that the rest-spread is what re-parents it before the repository's plain-object check. Measured in the real image, that is stale: body-parser 2.3.0 routes both extended and non-extended parsing through qs.parse, so extended:false now only sets depth:0 and node:querystring is never involved. The prototype is Object.prototype and the raw body would have been accepted. The spread stays for a different and real reason — next must be split out or the repository's key allowlist rejects it — and a case pins that reason rather than the stale one. This is the second time in two tasks that a planner's stated MECHANISM was wrong while the conclusion held, which is worth noticing: a correct instruction resting on a false premise survives implementation and dies later, when someone edits the code the premise justified.

RECIPE F3 CAME OUT NARROWER, and the explanation is worth more than the recipe. Only one case notices the return-path validator is gone, because when validation is removed the URL composition step silently absorbs a rejected absolute target into a relative one. So the open redirect is guarded by exactly one case, and the composition step is not a second layer — it is a mask. The reviewer should decide whether one case is enough there.

DEVIATION 1 IS A PLAN OMISSION, not an implementer choice: a literal in the route-discovery test moves and section 5.1 does not list it. Without moving it the suite is red, and it is exactly what makes the mount recipe's predicted count come out. Owen should add it to section 5.1.

REVIEW: assigning agent:qa-ruben. Lena implemented, so implementer != reviewer holds. Ruben over Priya on rotation and on fit — she reviewed AS-42 an hour ago and this task's ownership falsifier exists because of what she found there, so a reader with no stake in that finding is the better check on whether the falsifier actually falsifies.
